conflicts.point: Whether mandatory pre-deployment certification by federal agencies is necessary to prevent disparate impact, or whether it creates administrative bottlenecks that stifle market innovation and credit access.

positions.stance: Supports mandatory pre-deployment certification to prevent unmitigated disparate impact from entering public markets.
Opposes pre-deployment certification as an administrative bottleneck that protects incumbents and restricts credit access.

conflicts.point: Whether continuous post-deployment telemetry and high-frequency optimization successfully eliminate disparate impact faster than static reviews, or whether they merely mask historical bias under new numerical weights.

positions.stance: Maintains that high-frequency optimization loops rapidly correct predictive drift and reduce lending disparities in real time.
Argues that internal metric optimization against contaminated training data merely refines proxy variables rather than removing underlying demographic skews.

verdicts.conflict: Whether mandatory pre-deployment certification by federal agencies is necessary to prevent disparate impact, or whether it creates administrative bottlenecks that stifle market innovation and credit access.
verdicts.rationale: Neither side provides empirical data quantifying the exact trade-off between prevented discrimination incidents and delayed credit access. The safetyist argument relies on theoretical feedback-loop contamination, while the accelerationist claim assumes live optimization corrects drift without proving it removes historical skews. Both positions lack longitudinal deployment studies.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Longitudinal audits comparing bias rates in markets with pre-approval rules versus markets with continuous monitoring would tip the balance.

verdicts.conflict: Whether continuous post-deployment telemetry and high-frequency optimization successfully eliminate disparate impact faster than static reviews, or whether they merely mask historical bias under new numerical weights.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist critique holds greater logical consistency because optimizing a model against historical training data that encodes past bias preserves underlying demographic skews through proxy variables. The accelerationist claim assumes mathematical optimization removes bias without explaining how objective functions trained on skewed inputs learn unbiased baseline distributions.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Demonstration that unsupervised optimization routines successfully recover unbiased demographic parity from historically contaminated training sets would validate the accelerationist model.
